The savings plan you can see: time, contributions and compounding

Use three charts and editable scenarios to see how regular saving, the starting date and return assumptions change a long-term goal.

Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

A savings plan has several adjustable parts. Begin with the contribution and time horizon you can sustain, then test a range of returns.

01

Read the gap between saving and growth

The first chart separates money contributed from the portfolio’s modeled value. The contribution line includes your initial savings and each monthly deposit. The difference between the lines is growth under the selected return assumption. With a negative return, that difference can be a loss.

The curve is a mathematical illustration. It does not show the path of a real investment. Markets do not supply a smooth annual return, and an account can lose value even while you continue contributing. The Investor.gov compound-interest calculator also treats initial capital, contributions, time and the estimated rate as distinct inputs.

Try setting the return to zero. The two lines should coincide. This is a useful baseline: the plan’s progress then comes entirely from your own deposits, making the required saving effort visible.

02

Compare the same finish date

The second chart compares starting monthly contributions now with delaying them by five or ten years. All cases share the selected finish date, contribution amount and return. Existing starting savings remain invested in every case. The delayed cases skip deposits rather than making larger catch-up payments later.

This comparison changes both the amount contributed and the time each deposit has to grow. It should not be interpreted as a pure investment-performance comparison. Starting sooner can improve the modeled endpoint at a positive return, but it also requires setting money aside sooner.

A practical follow-up is to ask what would make an earlier start feasible: a smaller initial transfer, redirecting an expense, or a gradual increase as income changes. A larger assumed return can make a spreadsheet balance without making the required outcome reliable.

03

Use the matrix as a stress test

The matrix varies the horizon and return while preserving your selected initial savings and monthly contribution. Each cell is an alternative scenario. Darker shading means a larger ending amount; it does not mean the outcome is more likely.

For a goal with a firm deadline, read down one time column and compare several rates. For a flexible goal, compare what additional time might accomplish. Keep the return convention consistent: these are nominal returns before tax, fees and inflation.

If only the most optimistic cell meets the goal, identify the funding gap. Possible changes include increasing contributions, changing the goal, delaying the deadline or finding other resources. Taking more risk creates a wider range of possible results; it does not guarantee the higher cell.

04

Know exactly how the example compounds

The annual return is an effective rate. The equivalent monthly rate is (1 + annual return)1/12 − 1. Each month, the existing balance grows by that rate and a deposit arrives at month-end. Using annual return divided by 12 would represent a different rate convention.

For an initial amount B, monthly deposit C, monthly rate m and N months, the ending value is B(1 + m)N + C[(1 + m)N − 1] ÷ m. When m is zero, use B + CN. The tool uses a month-by-month recurrence, which also handles delayed deposits explicitly.

Real account results depend on actual deposit dates, changing returns, costs and tax treatment. This calculator does not impose contribution limits or determine account eligibility. Use the relevant current account rules when turning an illustration into an implemented plan.

05

Translate the chart into a monthly decision

  1. Describe the goal in today’s dollars and give it a date.
  2. Separate near-term cash needs from money that can remain invested.
  3. Choose a contribution that fits actual cash flow.
  4. Test a lower-return scenario and an interruption in deposits.
  5. Review progress as income, prices and the goal change.

The ending balance is only one planning measure. Also record how much money you must contribute, whether the schedule leaves a cash reserve, and how flexible the goal is. Read the inflation guide next to translate a future balance into purchasing power.
